identity.title: The Coverage Principle: How Pre-Training Enables Post-Training

problem.claim: Explain how pre-training shapes the success of post-training and downstream performance.

gap.claim: Existing understanding is limited, and cross-entropy loss may poorly predict downstream performance.

contributions.claim: Introduces coverage as a lens for analyzing post-training and Best-of-N success, characterizing it as necessary and sufficient for these methods to succeed.
Develops an account of why next-token prediction implicitly optimizes for good coverage and why coverage predicts downstream performance faster than cross entropy.
Studies model/checkpoint selection, gradient normalization, and test-time decoding strategies with stated provable benefits for improving coverage.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present a coverage-based theoretical perspective and identify a mechanism linking coverage's predictive power to faster generalization than cross entropy.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that coverage generalizes faster than cross entropy and avoids spurious dependence on problem-dependent parameters such as sequence length.
The authors report provable benefits from practical interventions targeting coverage, including selection procedures, gradient normalization, and test-time decoding.

narrative_sequence.summary: Pre-training enables strong fine-tuned models, but its effect on final-model success is poorly understood.
Cross entropy is commonly used to quantify pre-training success but can poorly predict downstream performance.
The paper analyzes the relationship through coverage, the probability mass assigned to high-quality responses, and states its necessity and sufficiency for post-training and Best-of-N success.
It explains coverage's predictive advantage over cross entropy and studies three intervention families intended to improve coverage.

source_observation.claim: The paper contrasts a standard training metric, cross entropy, with coverage because the latter is reported to generalize faster and avoid sequence-length dependence.

lessons.interpretation: A task-relevant intermediate quantity can frame why a familiar objective fails to predict the desired outcome.
lessons.application: When motivating a new metric, explicitly identify the standard metric's predictive limitation and state the mechanism by which the proposed quantity addresses it.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the abstract lacks evidence that the proposed quantity connects to the target outcome or explains the limitation.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the formal assumptions, theorem statements, model scales, datasets, or quantitative magnitudes behind the coverage claims.
The scope of the stated necessity-and-sufficiency result across post-training and test-time methods is not detailed.
The abstract does not report empirical comparisons or conditions under which each intervention provides its provable benefit.
